Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let
$\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its normalized Haar integral
$dm_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).

**Characters.** For $k\in\mathbb Z$ define $e_k:\mathbb T\to\mathbb C$ by
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\,\widetilde x)$ for $x=[\widetilde x]\in\mathbb T$,
where $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-complex-exponential]]). The
definition is independent of the representative $\widetilde x$: replacing
$\widetilde x$ by $\widetilde x+n$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$ adds the period
$2\pi kn$ to the argument of sine and cosine. Each $e_k$ is continuous, hence
Borel, and satisfies

$$e_k(x)e_l(x)=e_{k+l}(x),\qquad |e_k(x)|=1,\qquad \overline{e_k(x)}=e_{-k}(x) ,$$

the last two by the cartesian form $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of
[[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and
[[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]. In particular $e_0=1$ and every
$e_k$ is bounded and nonzero everywhere.

**Fourier coefficients.** Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]), that is, a class
of Borel functions with $\int_{\mathbb T}|f|\,dm_{\mathbb T}<+\infty$. Define the
**Fourier coefficient** of $f$ at $k\in\mathbb Z$ by

$$\widehat f(k):=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)\exp(-2\pi ikx)\,dm_{\mathbb T}.$$

This is well defined: $|f\,e_{-k}|=|f|$ because $|e_{-k}|=1$, so
$f\,e_{-k}\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ and its integral is finite; and the
integral depends only on the class of $f$, because it is unchanged when $f$ is
modified on a null set
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). The map
$f\mapsto\widehat f(k)$ is complex-linear for each $k$
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

**Trigonometric polynomials.** A **trigonometric polynomial** on $\mathbb T$ is
a finite complex linear combination of characters, $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_ke_k$, for
a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and scalars $c_k\in\mathbb C$. The set of all
trigonometric polynomials is the span of $\{e_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; it is closed
under addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication and complex conjugation
(by the identities for $e_ke_l$ and $\overline{e_k}$), and it contains $e_0=1$.
Nothing is claimed here about uniqueness of the coefficients in an expansion,
nor about the size of $\widehat p$; those are properties of the characters
proved below.

**The finite torus.** On $\mathbb T^n$, $n\ge1$, the characters are
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, where $k\cdot x$ is the
Euclidean dot product of a representative tuple; trigonometric polynomials are
finite complex linear combinations of these, and Fourier coefficients of
$f\in L^1(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ are
$\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^n}f\,e_{-k}\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}$. Fubini computes
integrals of products of characters on the product measure
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ Hölder's inequality makes $f\,e_{-k}$
integrable ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]],
[[thm-finite-measure-l-r-includes-into-l-p-for-p-less-r]]).

and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert

2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), meaning every at most countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the normalized product Haar measure $dx$ with $dx(\mathbb T^d)=1$, and let $\rho_0$ be a real measurable function on $\mathbb T^d$ with $0\le\rho_0\le1$ almost everywhere. For a finite $T\ge0$, a **weak heat solution with datum $\rho_0$** is a family $(u_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ of real essentially bounded measurable-function classes (elements of $L^\infty(\mathbb T^d,dx;\mathbb R)$), with $u_0=\rho_0$ as a function class, such that for every complex-valued smooth periodic test function $G$, the map $t\mapsto\int_{\mathbb T^d}u_t(x)G(x)\,dx$ is continuous and

$$\int_{\mathbb T^d}u_t(x)G(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_0(x)G(x)\,dx+\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb T^d}u_s(x)\Delta G(x)\,dx\,ds$$

for every $0\le t\le T$. Here $\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^d\partial_{x_i}^2$ is the periodic Laplacian; equality of function classes means equality almost everywhere with respect to $dx$. For the Fourier convention on this torus, set $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ and $\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dx$ for $f\in L^1(\mathbb T^d,dx)$.

derivations.claim: Since $0\le\rho_0\le1$ and $dx(\mathbb T^d)=1$, $\rho_0\in L^1$ and $|\widehat\rho_0(k)|\le1$ for every $k$. For any smooth $G$ and integer $m\ge1$, periodic integration by parts gives $(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)^m\widehat G(k)=\widehat{(1-\Delta)^mG}(k)$, hence $|\widehat G(k)|\le\|(1-\Delta)^mG\|_{L^1}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)^{-m}$. If $q\ge0$ is fixed, choose $m>(d+q)/2$; grouping lattice points by $r=\|k\|_\infty$ gives at most $(2r+1)^d-(2r-1)^d\le C_dr^{d-1}$ points in shell $r$. The shell contribution to $\sum_k(1+|k|)^q|\widehat G(k)|$ is at most $C r^{d-1+q-2m}$. Grouping shells into dyadic blocks $2^j\le r<2^{j+1}$ bounds the $j$th block by $C'2^{j(d+q-2m)}$, a convergent geometric series since $2m>d+q$. Thus $\sum_k(1+|k|)^q|\widehat G(k)|<\infty$.

For each $t>0$ and each fixed derivative order, multiplication of the coefficients by any corresponding polynomial in $k$ still leaves an absolutely summable sequence, because $|\widehat\rho_0(k)|\le1$ and the Gaussian factor $e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}$ dominates every inverse power on lattice shells. Therefore the heat series and all fixed-order differentiated series converge uniformly on $\mathbb T^d$ for $t\ge\varepsilon>0$. Pairing the $k$ and $-k$ terms shows $\rho_t$ is real. Termwise differentiation is valid on every such compact time interval; both $\partial_t$ and $\Delta$ multiply the $k$th term by $-4\pi^2|k|^2$, so $\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta\rho_t$.

The decay estimate in step 1.1 makes the Fourier series for $G$ and for each fixed space or time derivative of $P_tG$ uniformly absolutely convergent even at $t=0$. By [F2], the series at $t=0$ equals $G$ in $L^2$; both are continuous, so equality almost everywhere implies equality everywhere. Uniform convergence of the differentiated series proves smoothness and uniform derivative bounds on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$. Also $\|P_tG-G\|_\infty\le\sum_k|\widehat G(k)|\,|e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}-1|\to0$ by splitting into a finite set of modes and an absolutely summable tail. Termwise differentiation gives $\partial_tP_tG=\Delta P_tG$.

Absolute convergence permits termwise integration against $\rho_0\in L^1$. Reindexing $k\mapsto-k$ and using the even multiplier $e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}$ gives $\int\rho_tG=\sum_k e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat\rho_0(k)\widehat G(-k)=\int\rho_0P_tG$. By step 2.2 this pairing tends to $\int\rho_0G$ as $t\downarrow0$. Differentiating the pairing for $t>0$ and using $\Delta P_tG=P_t\Delta G$ yields $\frac{d}{dt}\int\rho_tG=\int\rho_t\Delta G$; integration from $0$ proves the weak identity in [F3]. Thus the constructed family is a weak heat solution.

Parseval and the heat coefficients give $\|\rho_t-\rho_0\|_2^2=\sum_k|\widehat\rho_0(k)|^2|e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}-1|^2\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$: choose a finite set whose tail in the convergent series $\sum_k|\widehat\rho_0(k)|^2$ is small, then take the limit on that finite set. For $\epsilon>0$ put $a_\epsilon(z)=\frac12(1-z/\sqrt{z^2+\epsilon^2})$ and $\Phi_\epsilon(z)=\int_0^z\int_0^r a_\epsilon(q)\,dq\,dr$. Then $\Phi_\epsilon$ is smooth and convex, $\Phi_\epsilon(0)=\Phi_\epsilon'(0)=0$, and $0\le\Phi_\epsilon(z)\le z^2/2$. On any interval $[a,b]\subset(0,T]$, the heat equation, chain rule, and periodic integration by parts give $\int\Phi_\epsilon(\rho_b)-\int\Phi_\epsilon(\rho_a)=-\int_a^b\int\Phi_\epsilon''(\rho_s)\sum_{i=1}^d|\partial_{x_i}\rho_s|^2\,dx\,ds\le0$. For each real $z$, the defining double integral tends to $\frac12(z^-)^2$, where $z^-:=\max\{-z,0\}$; dominated convergence on the bounded range of $\rho$ over $[a,b]\times\mathbb T^d$ gives the same monotonicity for $\|\rho_t^-\|_2^2$. Letting $a\downarrow0$, the $L^2$ continuity just proved and $\rho_0\ge0$ imply $\rho_t^-=0$. The assumed datum already gives the required bound when $T=0$.

For the upper bound put $b_\epsilon(z)=\frac12(1+(z-1)/\sqrt{(z-1)^2+\epsilon^2})$ and $\Psi_\epsilon(z)=\int_1^z\int_1^r b_\epsilon(q)\,dq\,dr$. This is smooth and convex with $\Psi_\epsilon(1)=\Psi_\epsilon'(1)=0$ and $0\le\Psi_\epsilon(z)\le(z-1)^2/2$. The same integration by parts gives $\int\Psi_\epsilon(\rho_b)\le\int\Psi_\epsilon(\rho_a)$ for $0<a<b$, and $\Psi_\epsilon(z)\to\frac12((z-1)^+)^2$, where $r^+:=\max\{r,0\}$. Dominated convergence and $L^2$ continuity at zero, together with $\rho_0\le1$, give $(\rho_t-1)^+=0$. The zero Fourier coefficient is unchanged by the heat multiplier, so $\int\rho_t=\widehat\rho_0(0)=\int\rho_0$. The assumed datum already gives the bound when $T=0$.

Let $(u_t)$ be any weak heat solution in the sense of [F3]. Testing its weak identity with $e_{-k}$ shows $g_k(t):=\widehat u_t(k)$ is continuous and satisfies $g_k(t)=\widehat\rho_0(k)-4\pi^2|k|^2\int_0^t g_k(s)\,ds$. Hence $g_k$ is differentiable and solves $g_k'=-4\pi^2|k|^2g_k$, so $g_k(t)=e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat\rho_0(k)$, the coefficient of the constructed $\rho_t$. For each $t$, both functions are in $L^2$; equality of all Fourier coefficients and completeness in [F2] imply $u_t=\rho_t$ almost everywhere. Thus the weak heat solution is unique.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let
$\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its normalized Haar integral
$dm_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).

**Characters.** For $k\in\mathbb Z$ define $e_k:\mathbb T\to\mathbb C$ by
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\,\widetilde x)$ for $x=[\widetilde x]\in\mathbb T$,
where $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-complex-exponential]]). The
definition is independent of the representative $\widetilde x$: replacing
$\widetilde x$ by $\widetilde x+n$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$ adds the period
$2\pi kn$ to the argument of sine and cosine. Each $e_k$ is continuous, hence
Borel, and satisfies

$$e_k(x)e_l(x)=e_{k+l}(x),\qquad |e_k(x)|=1,\qquad \overline{e_k(x)}=e_{-k}(x) ,$$

the last two by the cartesian form $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of
[[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and
[[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]. In particular $e_0=1$ and every
$e_k$ is bounded and nonzero everywhere.

**Fourier coefficients.** Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]), that is, a class
of Borel functions with $\int_{\mathbb T}|f|\,dm_{\mathbb T}<+\infty$. Define the
**Fourier coefficient** of $f$ at $k\in\mathbb Z$ by

$$\widehat f(k):=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)\exp(-2\pi ikx)\,dm_{\mathbb T}.$$

This is well defined: $|f\,e_{-k}|=|f|$ because $|e_{-k}|=1$, so
$f\,e_{-k}\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ and its integral is finite; and the
integral depends only on the class of $f$, because it is unchanged when $f$ is
modified on a null set
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). The map
$f\mapsto\widehat f(k)$ is complex-linear for each $k$
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

**Trigonometric polynomials.** A **trigonometric polynomial** on $\mathbb T$ is
a finite complex linear combination of characters, $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_ke_k$, for
a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and scalars $c_k\in\mathbb C$. The set of all
trigonometric polynomials is the span of $\{e_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; it is closed
under addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication and complex conjugation
(by the identities for $e_ke_l$ and $\overline{e_k}$), and it contains $e_0=1$.
Nothing is claimed here about uniqueness of the coefficients in an expansion,
nor about the size of $\widehat p$; those are properties of the characters
proved below.

**The finite torus.** On $\mathbb T^n$, $n\ge1$, the characters are
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, where $k\cdot x$ is the
Euclidean dot product of a representative tuple; trigonometric polynomials are
finite complex linear combinations of these, and Fourier coefficients of
$f\in L^1(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ are
$\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^n}f\,e_{-k}\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}$. Fubini computes
integrals of products of characters on the product measure
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ Hölder's inequality makes $f\,e_{-k}$
integrable ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]],
[[thm-finite-measure-l-r-includes-into-l-p-for-p-less-r]]).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A **finite reversible stochastic rate model** consists of an integer $r\ge2$, the finite state set $E=\{1,\ldots,r\}$, real energy parameters $e_a\in\mathbb R$, an inverse-energy parameter $\beta>0$, and finite transition rates $w_{ab}\ge0$ for distinct $a,b\in E$. When physical units are assigned, $e_a$ is measured in joules, $\beta$ in joules$^{-1}$, and $w_{ab}$ in seconds$^{-1}$; this mathematical definition does not assert a physical realization. Define

$$Z:=\sum_{a\in E}e^{-\beta e_a},\qquad \pi_a:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta e_a}.$$

Then $Z$ is finite and positive, and $\pi$ is a strictly positive probability vector. Require $w_{ab}>0$ exactly when $w_{ba}>0$, require the undirected graph with edge $\{a,b\}$ whenever $w_{ab}>0$ to be connected, and impose detailed balance $\pi_aw_{ab}=\pi_bw_{ba}$. Define the row generator $Q$ by $Q_{ab}=w_{ab}$ for $a\ne b$ and $Q_{aa}=-q_a$, where $q_a:=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}$. Since $r\ge2$ and the graph is connected, every $q_a>0$. Thus $(Qf)_a=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}(f_b-f_a)$ for a column observable $f$, and a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pQ$.

For any observable $f:E\to\mathbb R$, write $\pi(f):=\sum_{a\in E}\pi_af_a$. For $f,g:E\to\mathbb R$, define $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi:=\sum_{a\in E}\pi_af_ag_a$. Since $E$ is finite and every $\pi_a>0$, all real functions on $E$ belong to this finite-dimensional real inner-product space, denoted $L^2(E,\pi)$; equality in it is pointwise equality.

The associated jump-chain construction waits an exponential time of rate $q_a$ in state $a$ and then selects state $b\ne a$ with probability $w_{ab}/q_a$, using fresh independent random choices at successive jumps. Here an exponential time of rate $q>0$ has survival probability $\Pr(\tau>t)=e^{-qt}$ for $t\ge0$. The Ionescu–Tulcea construction [[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]] supplies the countable random sequence under the stated Choice assumption. The theorem on this page proves nonexplosion, identifies the transition semigroup, and establishes the positive reversible spectral gap. This is a finite mathematical rate model, not a derivation of rates from Hamiltonian mechanics.

Let $E=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for a finite integer $m\ge1$. A rate matrix on $E$ is a real matrix $L=(L_{ij})_{i,j\in E}$ such that $L_{ij}\ge0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\sum_{j\in E}L_{ij}=0$ for every $i$. Write $\lambda_i=\sum_{j\ne i}L_{ij}$, so $L_{ii}=-\lambda_i$. The row convention acts on a column observable $f:E\to\mathbb R$ by $(Lf)(i)=\sum_jL_{ij}f(j)$; a row probability vector evolves by right multiplication.

Fix an initial probability vector $\nu$ on $E$ and put $q=\max_i\lambda_i$. If $q=0$, then $L=0$ and the associated realization is the constant process $X_t=Y_0$ with $Y_0\sim\nu$. If $q>0$, put $R=I+L/q$, a stochastic matrix. A uniformized realization consists of a probability space carrying a discrete-time Markov sequence $(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ with initial law $\nu$ and transition matrix $R$, and independent random variables $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ that are independent of the entire sequence $Y$ and satisfy $\mathbb P(W_n>u)=e^{-qu}$ for $u\ge0$. Here a discrete-time Markov sequence with transition matrix $R$ means that
$$\mathbb P(A\cap\{Y_{n+1}=j\})=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A R_{Y_nj}]$$
for every $n\ge0$, $j\in E$, and $A\in\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)$. Each $W_n$ therefore has the exponential distribution of rate $q$; in particular its mean is $q^{-1}$. Require $\sum_{n\ge1}W_n=+\infty$ almost surely. Put $T_0=0$, $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nW_k$, and, on this probability-one event, $N_t=\max\{n:T_n\le t\}$ and $X_t=Y_{N_t}$. On its null complement set $N_t=0$ and $X_t=Y_0$. The construction filtration is $\mathcal F_t=\sigma(N_s,X_s:0\le s\le t)$; it records event counts and states through time $t$ and is not completed or made right-continuous by this definition.

This uniformized construction permits reducible rate matrices and states with zero exit rate. A local existence result proves that every finite rate matrix and initial law admit such a realization and that its conditional transition matrices are $e^{tL}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^nL^n/n!$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, meaning every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and an integer $N\ge3$. Let $\Lambda_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$, with each coordinate represented by $0,1,\ldots,N-1$, and let $\mathcal E_N$ be the set of unordered nearest-neighbor bonds $\{x,x+e_i\}$, where $1\le i\le d$ and addition is modulo $N$. The condition $N\ge3$ makes this a simple graph with each bond listed once as $x$ ranges over $\Lambda_N$. The site graph is connected because any two coordinate tuples are joined by finitely many steps of $+e_i$ or $-e_i$.

The configuration space is $\Omega_N=\{\eta:\Lambda_N\to\{0,1\}\}$, ordered lexicographically by its binary occupation vector in the fixed site order; this labels it as a finite set $\{1,\ldots,2^{N^d}\}$. The occupation $\eta_x$ is $1$ for an occupied site and $0$ for a vacant site. For $b=\{x,y\}\in\mathcal E_N$, let $\eta^b$ be the configuration obtained by swapping $\eta_x$ and $\eta_y$.

The coordinates $x/N$ have dimensionless spacing $1/N$ on the unit torus, and $t$ is dimensionless diffusive time: it is the microscopic unit-rate bond clock accelerated by the factor $N^2$. Thus the continuum heat equation below has normalized diffusion coefficient $D=1$.

Define a rate matrix $L_N$ on $\Omega_N$ by giving each distinct state change $\eta\to\eta^b\ne\eta$ rate $N^2$ and setting the diagonal entry to the negative sum of the off-diagonal row. If the two occupations on a bond agree, swapping them produces no state change and contributes no off-diagonal transition. On a column observable $f:\Omega_N\to\mathbb R$, use the row-generator convention $(L_Nf)(\eta)=\sum_{\xi\ne\eta}L_N(\eta,\xi)(f(\xi)-f(\eta))$; a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pL_N$. The **symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP)** is the uniformized finite-state chain with rate matrix $L_N$ and any specified initial probability vector. The finite-generator existence result supplies its all-pairs transition matrices $e^{tL_N}$ and càdlàg paths. Every jump conserves $\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x$.

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N^d$, the fixed-occupancy sector is $\Omega_{N,k}=\{\eta\in\Omega_N:\sum_x\eta_x=k\}$. When $0<k<N^d$, this sector has at least two states and its transition graph is connected by the fixed-occupancy connectivity lemma. Setting every sector energy to $0$, $\beta=1$, and each allowed transition rate to $N^2$ makes this sector a finite reversible stochastic rate model with uniform stationary weights. The sectors $k=0$ and $k=N^d$ are singleton constant chains. The full SSEP state graph is reducible across particle-number sectors; the generic finite rate-matrix construction, not the irreducible reversible-model definition, defines the full process.

Let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized Haar measure $dx$. For $x\in\Lambda_N$, write $x/N\in\mathbb T^d$ for the point with coordinates represented in $[0,1)$. The empirical measure and its action on a smooth periodic test function $G$ are

$$\pi_t^N:=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)\,\delta_{x/N},\qquad \langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^d}G\,d\pi_t^N=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)G(x/N).$$

Here $\delta_y$ denotes unit point mass at $y$. Thus $\pi_t^N$ is a finite positive measure of total mass at most $1$, not necessarily a probability measure. For a smooth periodic $G$, define its discrete Laplacian on grid points by

$$\Delta_NG(x/N):=N^2\sum_{i=1}^d\bigl[G((x+e_i)/N)+G((x-e_i)/N)-2G(x/N)\bigr].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $E$ be finite and nonempty, let $L$ be a rate matrix on $E$, let $X$ be its uniformized realization from the preceding existence result, and let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Put $g=Lf$ and
$$M_t=f(X_t)-f(X_0)-\int_0^t g(X_s)\,ds,\qquad \Gamma_f(i)=L(f^2)(i)-2f(i)Lf(i).$$For every finite $T$, $(M_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ is a square-integrable martingale relative to the construction filtration, and$$A_t:=\int_0^t\Gamma_f(X_s)\,ds$$
is its continuous predictable bracket: $A_0=0$, $A$ is increasing and predictable, and $M_t^2-A_t$ is a martingale. The bracket is understood in the continuous predictable increasing compensator convention stated in the proof.

derivations.claim: Put $f_G(\eta)=N^{-d}\sum_x\eta_xG(x/N)$. For the bond $\{x,x+e_i\}$, $f_G(\eta^{x,x+e_i})-f_G(\eta)=N^{-d}(\eta_{x+e_i}-\eta_x)(G(x/N)-G((x+e_i)/N))$. Summing its rate-$N^2$ contribution over all $x,i$ and reindexing the terms containing $\eta_{x+e_i}$ gives $L_Nf_G(\eta)=N^{-d}\sum_x\eta_xN^2\sum_i[G((x+e_i)/N)+G((x-e_i)/N)-2G(x/N)]=\langle\pi^N(\eta),\Delta_NG\rangle$. Thus the finite-chain martingale in [F2], applied to $f_G$, is exactly $M_t^{N,G}$ and has bracket given by the sum of rates times squared jumps.

A bond with equal endpoint occupations has zero jump; otherwise its squared jump is $N^{-2d}(G((x+e_i)/N)-G(x/N))^2$. Substituting these jumps and rate $N^2$ into [F2] gives the displayed bracket. By the fundamental theorem of calculus along the coordinate segment, $|G((x+e_i)/N)-G(x/N)|\le N^{-1}\|\partial_iG\|_\infty$, while $(\eta_{x+e_i}-\eta_x)^2\le1$. There are $N^d$ bonds in each coordinate direction, so the bracket is increasing, continuous, predictable, and bounded by $TN^{-d}\sum_i\|\partial_iG\|_\infty^2$. The finite state space makes $f_G$ bounded, hence [F2] also gives square integrability.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, meaning every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and an integer $N\ge3$. Let $\Lambda_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$, with each coordinate represented by $0,1,\ldots,N-1$, and let $\mathcal E_N$ be the set of unordered nearest-neighbor bonds $\{x,x+e_i\}$, where $1\le i\le d$ and addition is modulo $N$. The condition $N\ge3$ makes this a simple graph with each bond listed once as $x$ ranges over $\Lambda_N$. The site graph is connected because any two coordinate tuples are joined by finitely many steps of $+e_i$ or $-e_i$.

The configuration space is $\Omega_N=\{\eta:\Lambda_N\to\{0,1\}\}$, ordered lexicographically by its binary occupation vector in the fixed site order; this labels it as a finite set $\{1,\ldots,2^{N^d}\}$. The occupation $\eta_x$ is $1$ for an occupied site and $0$ for a vacant site. For $b=\{x,y\}\in\mathcal E_N$, let $\eta^b$ be the configuration obtained by swapping $\eta_x$ and $\eta_y$.

The coordinates $x/N$ have dimensionless spacing $1/N$ on the unit torus, and $t$ is dimensionless diffusive time: it is the microscopic unit-rate bond clock accelerated by the factor $N^2$. Thus the continuum heat equation below has normalized diffusion coefficient $D=1$.

Define a rate matrix $L_N$ on $\Omega_N$ by giving each distinct state change $\eta\to\eta^b\ne\eta$ rate $N^2$ and setting the diagonal entry to the negative sum of the off-diagonal row. If the two occupations on a bond agree, swapping them produces no state change and contributes no off-diagonal transition. On a column observable $f:\Omega_N\to\mathbb R$, use the row-generator convention $(L_Nf)(\eta)=\sum_{\xi\ne\eta}L_N(\eta,\xi)(f(\xi)-f(\eta))$; a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pL_N$. The **symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP)** is the uniformized finite-state chain with rate matrix $L_N$ and any specified initial probability vector. The finite-generator existence result supplies its all-pairs transition matrices $e^{tL_N}$ and càdlàg paths. Every jump conserves $\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x$.

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N^d$, the fixed-occupancy sector is $\Omega_{N,k}=\{\eta\in\Omega_N:\sum_x\eta_x=k\}$. When $0<k<N^d$, this sector has at least two states and its transition graph is connected by the fixed-occupancy connectivity lemma. Setting every sector energy to $0$, $\beta=1$, and each allowed transition rate to $N^2$ makes this sector a finite reversible stochastic rate model with uniform stationary weights. The sectors $k=0$ and $k=N^d$ are singleton constant chains. The full SSEP state graph is reducible across particle-number sectors; the generic finite rate-matrix construction, not the irreducible reversible-model definition, defines the full process.

Let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized Haar measure $dx$. For $x\in\Lambda_N$, write $x/N\in\mathbb T^d$ for the point with coordinates represented in $[0,1)$. The empirical measure and its action on a smooth periodic test function $G$ are

$$\pi_t^N:=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)\,\delta_{x/N},\qquad \langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^d}G\,d\pi_t^N=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)G(x/N).$$

Here $\delta_y$ denotes unit point mass at $y$. Thus $\pi_t^N$ is a finite positive measure of total mass at most $1$, not necessarily a probability measure. For a smooth periodic $G$, define its discrete Laplacian on grid points by

$$\Delta_NG(x/N):=N^2\sum_{i=1}^d\bigl[G((x+e_i)/N)+G((x-e_i)/N)-2G(x/N)\bigr].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Fix $N$ and a state $i=\eta_s$. By [F2], on an interval of length $h$, two or more potential uniformization events have probability $O_N(h^2)$, one actual transition $i\to j$ has probability $hL_N(i,j)+O_N(h^2)$, and no state change has probability $1-h\lambda_i+O_N(h^2)$, with $\lambda_i=\sum_{j\ne i}L_N(i,j)$. Taylor expansion is uniform over the finite state set and $s\in[0,T]$. If no state change occurs, then $F_{s+h}^N(i)-F_s^N(i)=h\partial_sF_s^N(i)+O_N(h^2)$ and the compensating integral is $h(\partial_sF_s^N+L_NF_s^N)(i)+O_N(h^2)$, so the increment of $M^N$ is $-hL_NF_s^N(i)+O_N(h^2)$. A single transition $i\to j$ gives increment $F_s^N(j)-F_s^N(i)+O_N(h)$; summing its conditional mean over $j$ gives $hL_NF_s^N(i)+O_N(h^2)$, which cancels the no-transition term. Paths with at least two potential events contribute $O_N(h^2)$ because $M^N$ has bounded increments for fixed $N,T$. Therefore $|\mathbb E[M_{s+h}^N-M_s^N\mid\mathcal F_s]|\le C_Nh^2$. In the conditional second moment, no transition contributes $O_N(h^2)$, one transition contributes $h\sum_{j\ne i}L_N(i,j)(F_s^N(j)-F_s^N(i))^2+O_N(h^2)=h\Gamma_{F_s^N}(i)+O_N(h^2)$, and two or more potential events contribute $O_N(h^2)$.

If $T=0$, the only time is $0$ and $M_0^N=0$. For $T>0$, fix $s<t$ and partition $[s,t]$ into $n$ equal intervals of length $h=(t-s)/n$. Applying the conditional-mean estimate from step 2.1 on every subinterval, then the tower property, bounds $|\mathbb E[M_t^N-M_s^N\mid\mathcal F_s]|$ by $nC_Nh^2\to0$. Thus $M^N$ is an all-pairs martingale. For fixed $N$ its paths are bounded on $[0,T]$ because the state space is finite, $H$ and its time derivative are bounded, and the compensating integrand is bounded; hence it is square-integrable.

Set $\gamma_s(\eta)=\Gamma_{F_s^N}(\eta)$ and $A_t^N=\int_0^t\gamma_s(\eta_s)ds$. If $T=0$, both processes are zero. For $T>0$, the second-moment expansion in step 2.1 and continuity of $\gamma_s(i)$ in $s$ imply $\mathbb E[A_{s+h}^N-A_s^N\mid\mathcal F_s]=h\gamma_s(\eta_s)+O_N(h^2)$: without a state change the integrand differs from $\gamma_s(\eta_s)$ by $O_N(h)$, and a state change has probability $O_N(h)$ and changes the bounded integrand over an interval of length $h$. Hence $\mathbb E[(M_{s+h}^N-M_s^N)^2-(A_{s+h}^N-A_s^N)\mid\mathcal F_s]=O_N(h^2)$. For fixed $s<t$, partition $[s,t]$ into $n$ equal intervals and write $\Delta_jM=M_{t_{j+1}}^N-M_{t_j}^N$, $\Delta_jA=A_{t_{j+1}}^N-A_{t_j}^N$. Since $M^N$ is a martingale, $\mathbb E[M_{t_j}^N\Delta_jM\mid\mathcal F_s]=0$ by the tower property. Expanding the square, conditioning each remainder $\Delta_jM^2-\Delta_jA$ first on $\mathcal F_{t_j}$, and using the bound just proved gives an absolute conditional expectation at most $nC_Nh^2\to0$. Therefore $(M_t^N)^2-A_t^N$ is an all-pairs martingale.

The integrand $\gamma_s(\eta_s)$ is nonnegative, so $A^N$ is increasing; it is continuous and adapted. If $T=0$, the zero process is predictable. Otherwise, for each nested deterministic partition, the process equal to $A^N$ at the left endpoint on each interval $(a,b]$ and zero at time zero is predictable by [F4]; these processes converge pointwise to $A^N$ by continuity. Thus $A^N$ is predictable. At a bond $\{x,x+e_i\}$, the test-function jump is $N^{-d}(\eta_{x+e_i}-\eta_x)(H(s,x/N)-H(s,(x+e_i)/N))$. Multiplying its square by the rate $N^2$ and summing over all bonds yields the displayed formula for $\gamma_s(\eta_s)$. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives $|H(s,(x+e_i)/N)-H(s,x/N)|\le N^{-1}\|\partial_iH(s,\cdot)\|_\infty$; using $(\eta_{x+e_i}-\eta_x)^2\le1$ and $N^d$ bonds per coordinate gives the stated bound for $A_T^N$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, meaning every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and an integer $N\ge3$. Let $\Lambda_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$, with each coordinate represented by $0,1,\ldots,N-1$, and let $\mathcal E_N$ be the set of unordered nearest-neighbor bonds $\{x,x+e_i\}$, where $1\le i\le d$ and addition is modulo $N$. The condition $N\ge3$ makes this a simple graph with each bond listed once as $x$ ranges over $\Lambda_N$. The site graph is connected because any two coordinate tuples are joined by finitely many steps of $+e_i$ or $-e_i$.

The configuration space is $\Omega_N=\{\eta:\Lambda_N\to\{0,1\}\}$, ordered lexicographically by its binary occupation vector in the fixed site order; this labels it as a finite set $\{1,\ldots,2^{N^d}\}$. The occupation $\eta_x$ is $1$ for an occupied site and $0$ for a vacant site. For $b=\{x,y\}\in\mathcal E_N$, let $\eta^b$ be the configuration obtained by swapping $\eta_x$ and $\eta_y$.

The coordinates $x/N$ have dimensionless spacing $1/N$ on the unit torus, and $t$ is dimensionless diffusive time: it is the microscopic unit-rate bond clock accelerated by the factor $N^2$. Thus the continuum heat equation below has normalized diffusion coefficient $D=1$.

Define a rate matrix $L_N$ on $\Omega_N$ by giving each distinct state change $\eta\to\eta^b\ne\eta$ rate $N^2$ and setting the diagonal entry to the negative sum of the off-diagonal row. If the two occupations on a bond agree, swapping them produces no state change and contributes no off-diagonal transition. On a column observable $f:\Omega_N\to\mathbb R$, use the row-generator convention $(L_Nf)(\eta)=\sum_{\xi\ne\eta}L_N(\eta,\xi)(f(\xi)-f(\eta))$; a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pL_N$. The **symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP)** is the uniformized finite-state chain with rate matrix $L_N$ and any specified initial probability vector. The finite-generator existence result supplies its all-pairs transition matrices $e^{tL_N}$ and càdlàg paths. Every jump conserves $\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x$.

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N^d$, the fixed-occupancy sector is $\Omega_{N,k}=\{\eta\in\Omega_N:\sum_x\eta_x=k\}$. When $0<k<N^d$, this sector has at least two states and its transition graph is connected by the fixed-occupancy connectivity lemma. Setting every sector energy to $0$, $\beta=1$, and each allowed transition rate to $N^2$ makes this sector a finite reversible stochastic rate model with uniform stationary weights. The sectors $k=0$ and $k=N^d$ are singleton constant chains. The full SSEP state graph is reducible across particle-number sectors; the generic finite rate-matrix construction, not the irreducible reversible-model definition, defines the full process.

Let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized Haar measure $dx$. For $x\in\Lambda_N$, write $x/N\in\mathbb T^d$ for the point with coordinates represented in $[0,1)$. The empirical measure and its action on a smooth periodic test function $G$ are

$$\pi_t^N:=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)\,\delta_{x/N},\qquad \langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^d}G\,d\pi_t^N=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)G(x/N).$$

Here $\delta_y$ denotes unit point mass at $y$. Thus $\pi_t^N$ is a finite positive measure of total mass at most $1$, not necessarily a probability measure. For a smooth periodic $G$, define its discrete Laplacian on grid points by

$$\Delta_NG(x/N):=N^2\sum_{i=1}^d\bigl[G((x+e_i)/N)+G((x-e_i)/N)-2G(x/N)\bigr].$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, meaning every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and an integer $N\ge3$. Let $\Lambda_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$, with each coordinate represented by $0,1,\ldots,N-1$, and let $\mathcal E_N$ be the set of unordered nearest-neighbor bonds $\{x,x+e_i\}$, where $1\le i\le d$ and addition is modulo $N$. The condition $N\ge3$ makes this a simple graph with each bond listed once as $x$ ranges over $\Lambda_N$. The site graph is connected because any two coordinate tuples are joined by finitely many steps of $+e_i$ or $-e_i$.

The configuration space is $\Omega_N=\{\eta:\Lambda_N\to\{0,1\}\}$, ordered lexicographically by its binary occupation vector in the fixed site order; this labels it as a finite set $\{1,\ldots,2^{N^d}\}$. The occupation $\eta_x$ is $1$ for an occupied site and $0$ for a vacant site. For $b=\{x,y\}\in\mathcal E_N$, let $\eta^b$ be the configuration obtained by swapping $\eta_x$ and $\eta_y$.

The coordinates $x/N$ have dimensionless spacing $1/N$ on the unit torus, and $t$ is dimensionless diffusive time: it is the microscopic unit-rate bond clock accelerated by the factor $N^2$. Thus the continuum heat equation below has normalized diffusion coefficient $D=1$.

Define a rate matrix $L_N$ on $\Omega_N$ by giving each distinct state change $\eta\to\eta^b\ne\eta$ rate $N^2$ and setting the diagonal entry to the negative sum of the off-diagonal row. If the two occupations on a bond agree, swapping them produces no state change and contributes no off-diagonal transition. On a column observable $f:\Omega_N\to\mathbb R$, use the row-generator convention $(L_Nf)(\eta)=\sum_{\xi\ne\eta}L_N(\eta,\xi)(f(\xi)-f(\eta))$; a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pL_N$. The **symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP)** is the uniformized finite-state chain with rate matrix $L_N$ and any specified initial probability vector. The finite-generator existence result supplies its all-pairs transition matrices $e^{tL_N}$ and càdlàg paths. Every jump conserves $\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x$.

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N^d$, the fixed-occupancy sector is $\Omega_{N,k}=\{\eta\in\Omega_N:\sum_x\eta_x=k\}$. When $0<k<N^d$, this sector has at least two states and its transition graph is connected by the fixed-occupancy connectivity lemma. Setting every sector energy to $0$, $\beta=1$, and each allowed transition rate to $N^2$ makes this sector a finite reversible stochastic rate model with uniform stationary weights. The sectors $k=0$ and $k=N^d$ are singleton constant chains. The full SSEP state graph is reducible across particle-number sectors; the generic finite rate-matrix construction, not the irreducible reversible-model definition, defines the full process.

Let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized Haar measure $dx$. For $x\in\Lambda_N$, write $x/N\in\mathbb T^d$ for the point with coordinates represented in $[0,1)$. The empirical measure and its action on a smooth periodic test function $G$ are

$$\pi_t^N:=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)\,\delta_{x/N},\qquad \langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^d}G\,d\pi_t^N=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)G(x/N).$$

Here $\delta_y$ denotes unit point mass at $y$. Thus $\pi_t^N$ is a finite positive measure of total mass at most $1$, not necessarily a probability measure. For a smooth periodic $G$, define its discrete Laplacian on grid points by

$$\Delta_NG(x/N):=N^2\sum_{i=1}^d\bigl[G((x+e_i)/N)+G((x-e_i)/N)-2G(x/N)\bigr].$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let $\rho_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $0\le\rho_0\le1$ almost everywhere, using normalized product Haar measure $dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ define $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i k\cdot x)$ and $\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dx$. For $t>0$ set

$$\rho_t(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat\rho_0(k)e_k(x),$$

and at $t=0$ set $\rho_t=\rho_0$ as an almost-everywhere class. For smooth periodic $G$, define

$$P_tG(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat G(k)e_k(x)\quad(t>0),\qquad P_0G:=G.$$

Then on every strip $[\epsilon,T]\times\mathbb T^d$ with $0<\epsilon<T<\infty$, the series for $\rho_t$ and all its space and time derivatives converge absolutely and uniformly; in particular $\rho_t$ is real and smooth for each $t>0$ and $\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta\rho_t$. For every finite $T$ and every smooth $G$, $P_tG$ is smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$, satisfies $\partial_tP_tG=\Delta P_tG$, has uniformly bounded derivatives of every fixed order there, and $P_tG\to G$ uniformly as $t\downarrow0$. Moreover

$$\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_tG\,dx=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_0P_tG\,dx,$$

so $(\rho_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ is the unique weak heat solution with datum $\rho_0$ in the stated weak formulation. It preserves $0\le\rho_t\le1$ almost everywhere and the mass $\int\rho_t\,dx=\int\rho_0\,dx$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $N\ge3$, $T\ge0$, and let $(\eta_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be the SSEP from the diffusive-model definition. Let $H:[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$ be smooth up to the time endpoints, meaning all time and space derivatives used below extend continuously to $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$. Define

$$F_s^N(\eta):=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_xH(s,x/N),\qquad 0\le s\le T.$$

Then

$$M_t^N:=F_t^N(\eta_t)-F_0^N(\eta_0)-\int_0^t\langle\pi_s^N,\partial_sH(s,\cdot)+\Delta_NH(s,\cdot)\rangle\,ds$$

is a square-integrable martingale, and

$$A_t^N:=N^{2-2d}\int_0^t\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}(\eta_{x+e_i}(s)-\eta_x(s))^2\bigl(H(s,(x+e_i)/N)-H(s,x/N)\bigr)^2\,ds$$

$$A_T^N\le T N^{-d}\sum_{i=1}^d\sup_{0\le s\le T}\|\partial_iH(s,\cdot)\|_\infty^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $N\ge3$, $T\ge0$, and let $(\eta_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be the SSEP from the diffusive-model definition with any initial probability vector. For a real smooth periodic $G:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$, set

$$M_t^{N,G}:=\langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle-\langle\pi_0^N,G\rangle-\int_0^t\langle\pi_s^N,\Delta_NG\rangle\,ds.$$

Then $M^{N,G}$ is a square-integrable martingale. Its continuous predictable bracket is

$$A_t^{N,G}=N^{2-2d}\int_0^t\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}(\eta_{x+e_i}(s)-\eta_x(s))^2\bigl(G((x+e_i)/N)-G(x/N)\bigr)^2\,ds,$$

in the continuous predictable compensator convention of the finite-chain martingale supplier. In particular,

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T\ge0$, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, and let $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be an increasing family of sub-$\sigma$-algebras of $\mathcal F$. Let $(M_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a family of real random variables such that each $M_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable, $\mathbb E[M_t^2]<\infty$, $M_0=0$, and $\mathbb E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s$ almost surely for every $0\le s\le t\le T$. Suppose it has càdlàg paths almost surely, meaning there is a measurable event $\Omega_0\in\mathcal F$ with $\mathbb P(\Omega_0)=1$ such that, for every $\omega\in\Omega_0$, the path $t\mapsto M_t(\omega)$ is right-continuous on $[0,T)$ and has a finite left limit at every $t\in(0,T]$. Define
$$
D_T=\bigcup_{n\ge0}\{kT/2^n:0\le k\le2^n\},\qquad S_T=\sup_{t\in D_T}|M_t|.
$$
Then $S_T$ is measurable and agrees with the pathwise supremum $\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|$ on $\Omega_0$, and
$$
\mathbb E[S_T^2]\le4\,\mathbb E[|M_T|^2].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let $\rho_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $0\le\rho_0\le1$ almost everywhere, using normalized product Haar measure $dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ define $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i k\cdot x)$ and $\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dx$. For $t>0$ set

$$\rho_t(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat\rho_0(k)e_k(x),$$

and at $t=0$ set $\rho_t=\rho_0$ as an almost-everywhere class. For smooth periodic $G$, define

$$P_tG(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat G(k)e_k(x)\quad(t>0),\qquad P_0G:=G.$$

Then on every strip $[\epsilon,T]\times\mathbb T^d$ with $0<\epsilon<T<\infty$, the series for $\rho_t$ and all its space and time derivatives converge absolutely and uniformly; in particular $\rho_t$ is real and smooth for each $t>0$ and $\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta\rho_t$. For every finite $T$ and every smooth $G$, $P_tG$ is smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$, satisfies $\partial_tP_tG=\Delta P_tG$, has uniformly bounded derivatives of every fixed order there, and $P_tG\to G$ uniformly as $t\downarrow0$. Moreover

$$\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_tG\,dx=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_0P_tG\,dx,$$

so $(\rho_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ is the unique weak heat solution with datum $\rho_0$ in the stated weak formulation. It preserves $0\le\rho_t\le1$ almost everywhere and the mass $\int\rho_t\,dx=\int\rho_0\,dx$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T\ge0$, and for each integer $N\ge3$ let $(\eta_t^N)_{0\le t\le T}$ be the SSEP on $\Lambda_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$ with rate $N^2$ on each unordered nearest-neighbor bond, started from any initial probability vector on a probability space $(\Xi_N,\mathcal A_N,\mathbb P_N)$. Write $\pi_t^N=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x^N(t)\delta_{x/N}$ for its empirical measure. Suppose a measurable $\rho_0:\mathbb T^d\to[0,1]$ satisfies, for every real-valued smooth periodic $G$ and every $\epsilon>0$,

$$\mathbb P_N\!\left(\left|\langle\pi_0^N,G\rangle-\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_0(x)G(x)\,dx\right|>\epsilon\right)\longrightarrow0\qquad(N\to\infty),$$

where the probability spaces may depend on $N$. Let $\rho_t$ be the unique weak heat solution on $\mathbb T^d$ with initial datum $\rho_0$, defined by the Fourier heat profile. Then for every real-valued smooth periodic $G$ and every $\epsilon>0$,

$$\mathbb P_N\!\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}\left|\langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle-\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_t(x)G(x)\,dx\right|>\epsilon\right)\longrightarrow0\qquad(N\to\infty).$$
